questions.question: Your action is a 10-dimensional torque vector. What breaks if you try to act by argmax over Q(s, a)?
options: The Q values become unbounded above
There is no tractable argmax over a continuous action space
The Bellman equation stops holding for continuous actions
The discount has to be raised to exactly 1
questions.explanation: Value-based control has to enumerate actions to pick the best one. Parameterizing the policy directly replaces that search with a sample from a distribution.

questions.question: What does the policy gradient theorem say ∇J(θ) equals?
options: The gradient of the squared TD error, averaged over transitions
The expected return multiplied by the gradient of the value function
The expectation of G_t times ∇_θ log π_θ(a_t | s_t)
The gradient of the policy's entropy, scaled by the return
questions.explanation: The log-derivative trick converts the gradient of an expectation into an expectation of a gradient. That is what makes it estimable from sampled trajectories at all.

questions.question: For a softmax policy, ∇_θ log π_θ(a | s) with respect to the logits equals what?
options: onehot(a) minus π(· | s)
π(· | s) minus onehot(a)
onehot(a) scaled by π(a | s)
The logits minus their mean
questions.explanation: It is the score of the action you took minus its expected score under the policy. Note that it sums to zero across actions, which is why a state-only baseline drops out in expectation.

questions.question: Why weight step t by the reward-to-go G_t rather than by the whole trajectory's return G_0?
options: G_0 is a biased estimator while G_t is unbiased
Only G_t keeps the estimator on-policy
G_0 folds in rewards collected before a_t, which a_t cannot have caused
The log-derivative trick only applies to reward-to-go
questions.explanation: Both estimators are unbiased; the earlier rewards are just zero-mean noise attached to every gradient term. Dropping them is variance reduction that costs nothing.

questions.question: You subtract a learned V̂(s_t) from G_t before multiplying by the score. Why is the gradient still unbiased?
options: Because V̂ was trained by regression onto the same G_t values
Because E[b(s_t) · ∇ log π(a_t | s_t)] = 0 whenever b ignores a_t
Because the same number is subtracted from every action at that state
Because the resulting advantages are renormalized to zero mean
questions.explanation: The score function has zero mean under π, so anything constant across actions at that state multiplies out to zero. That freedom is what lets a critic cut variance without shifting the optimum.

questions.question: You read `loss = -advantage * log_prob` in a 2026 training script. What are you looking at?
options: A TD(0) value-regression loss
A cross-entropy loss for behavior cloning
A Q-learning bootstrap target
REINFORCE with a baseline
questions.explanation: The minus sign turns gradient ascent on J into descent on a loss, and the advantage is the baseline-subtracted return. PPO, GRPO, RLOO and DPO are all variance-reduction machinery bolted onto this one line.
